title: From Zombie Fungi to Fossil Birds: The Living Tributes to David Attenborough on His 100th Birthday
summary: David Attenborough's voice has guided millions through the wonders of the natural world. For many researchers, his documentaries were the spark that ignited a lifelong passion for biology. So it's no surprise that when they discover new species, they often honor the man who inspired them. By latest count, about 50 organisms—from orchids to marine worms to one of the earliest known predators—bear Attenborough's name. On May 8, he turned 100. To celebrate, here are a few of those living tributes. Consider *Gibellula attenboroughii*, a parasitic fungus that turns cave spiders into zombies. Described in 2025, it forces its reclusive hosts to leave their hiding spots and climb to exposed areas near cave entrances. There, the fungus erupts from the spider's body, releasing spores into the air currents. João Araújo of the Natural History Museum of Denmark, who helped name the species, credits Attenborough's segment on *Cordyceps* ants for steering his research toward these macabre fungi. Then there's *Imparavis attenboroughi*, a 120-million-year-old bird fossil from China. Unlike most early birds, it had no teeth—a trait previously thought to have evolved much later. The discovery, published in 2024, pushed back the timeline for toothlessness in birds by 48 million years. Lead researcher Alex Clark said Attenborough's documentaries were a direct reason he entered the natural sciences. Not all tributes are ancient or creepy. *Marphysa davidattenboroughi* is a shimmering, rainbow-hued bloodworm found off the coast of Australia. Nicolas Lavesque, the taxonomist who described it in 2023, recalls watching Attenborough's shows as a child. When he sent Attenborough the paper, the broadcaster replied with a handwritten note—a gesture that sent Lavesque's kids jumping for joy. These species, and dozens more, reflect a simple truth: Attenborough didn't just show us nature; he made us fall in love with it. As one scientist put it, he's been a huge voice for waking up to the planet's issues. And now, his name lives on in the very organisms he spent a lifetime celebrating.
why_it_matters: The species named after David Attenborough are a reminder that public science communication can spark entire careers and lead to real discoveries. For a 13-year-old who loves nature, it shows that inspiration can travel from a TV screen all the way to a researcher’s lab—and eventually into the scientific record, helping to catalogue the planet’s biodiversity before it vanishes.

background_read: David Attenborough (a British broadcaster and naturalist, born in 1926, whose series like *Planet Earth* and *Life on Earth* have been seen by billions) has spent a lifetime making the natural world accessible. Taxonomists—the scientists who discover and name new species—often honor people who inspired their work.

The tradition of naming species after notable figures goes back to Linnaeus, the 18th-century founder of modern classification. The International Code of Zoological Nomenclature allows a species to be named for a person as long as the description is formally published. Celebrities like Beyoncé (who has a horse fly named Scaptia beyonceae) and even Darth Vader (a beetle) have received the same tribute.

Attenborough’s count of about 50 species is exceptional and spans fungi, plants, insects, fish, and even an ancient predator. The three species highlighted here come from different corners of biology: a parasitic fungus that manipulates spider behaviour (related to the *Cordyceps* fungus Attenborough once showcased), a toothless fossil bird that rewrites dinosaur-era history, and a shimmering marine worm off Australia. They reflect how his documentaries nurtured biologists across the globe.

perspectives.description: Biologists who name species after Attenborough argue that it honors a man who made the natural world exciting for millions, and it draws public attention to newly discovered organisms. Linking a species to a beloved figure can boost interest in conservation and taxonomic research.

Some taxonomists worry that naming species after celebrities—rather than after the species' traits or local cultural names—can seem frivolous and distract from the urgent need to document biodiversity. They argue that limited resources and journal space are better used for purely scientific descriptions.

Naming species after people has been a standard taxonomic practice for centuries; it can reflect genuine gratitude and is regulated by international codes. The practice can make science feel more personal and accessible, even if it sometimes sparks debate about its seriousness.

As Attenborough’s career inspires new generations and climate change threatens biodiversity, future species named after conservationists could serve as permanent monuments. The living tributes may become not just a thank you, but also a call to action for the very ecosystems they come from.
